summary.title: The care and feeding of software engineers (or, why engineers are grumpy)
summary.one_liner: Software engineers seem grumpy because they are treated as short-order builders while seeing themselves as creators, and are hit by vague requirements, shifting priorities, underestimated timelines, and misplaced management fixes like adding more people.
keywords: adding more engineers to a late project
takeaways: Engineers feel like creators, but companies often treat them as implementers, which breeds resentment.
Vague requirements force engineers to make assumptions, and changing requirements invalidate that work, causing rework and burnout.
Frequent priority changes cause context switches that cut engineering productivity.
Time estimates tend to be too short because they ignore learning time, meetings, bugs, and changing requirements.
Adding engineers to a late project often makes it later because many tasks are sequential and coordination cost rises.
summary.summary: Nicholas Zakas, responding to Jenna Bilotta's article on designer-engineer collaboration, explains why software engineers have a reputation for being grumpy. He uses an extended house-building analogy to show how incomplete specifications lead engineers to make assumptions that later break. He also covers context switching, underestimated estimates driven by overconfidence and missing time for learning, the "I used to code" problem, and the failed idea that more engineers speed up late projects. The post is opinion and personal experience rather than a how-to, with no technical instructions.
